doc.title: Albert Warner and Sonny Henry Interview, 1959-01-08

title: First jobs with the Bulls Band and moving through New Orleans bands
summary: He describes his first jobs, then playing with Louis Dumaine, Columbia, Camellia, Chris Kelly and Kid Rena until he quit at the depression.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: The Depression years and the WPA band

blocks.x: With Pete there. So we'd go to the barbershop on Bienville Street there and we'd rehearsal up near him and I just the bass and the trombone. So this fella, Amos White. That's right. Amos White would come along and he'd join in with us and he would write off a little piece of music there and make me go over that music, you know, and so finally I got pretty good with it. And so this little band formed up as I went with them. They call it the Bulls Band. So I went on and started playing with them. So first job they had for carnival day, Steve say, well, I wasn't good enough. He wouldn't take me out. So the boys say, well, he says, you better take him, would you say you'll have some kind of help. So he went on out there and then he'd come out there. He fell down on the job. You see, the next job that he got was down at the Holy Ghost Church there, uh, Holy Redeemer down on Royal and Lysian Field. So I went on down there and I played this job with him and went back, back in the woods here somewhere as they had, they were shot at a trumpet player and they pick up a trumpet player back there. So this fella walked up to me, he says, where are you from? I said, I'm from New Orleans. I said, I never seen you before. I said, no, it's the first time I was out. He said, well, you say you, first time you was out. He said, I don't understand. He says, you playing as good as this fella. Yeah. And this is an old musician. I said, well, I said, that's my teacher. He said, your teacher, you done beat your teacher. I said, yeah. He said, yeah, you done beat your teacher. So, uh, after that, I just going from band to band after I got good, you know, and I'd started playing with, uh, the, uh, what do you call this fella? What you was calling it? Louis Demene and Eddie Jackson. So they sent downtown and got me, they were living uptown. So they said they wanted me to play with them. So I went on and started playing in a little, little band they had up there. No name to it, just the- Just Louis Demene and Eddie Jackson. That's all. See, so I went on to playing with them. So after this, I went with, left them, I went with, uh, fella by the name of William, the Columbia Band. See, and after I left the Columbia Band and I went on, I went with the Camellia Band. Well, the Camellia had a pretty good pull around this town here. They had work in the countries and down Violet and all those different plays, Boytranville. They was doing pretty good. Who was in there who was leader? Uh, Joe Nicholas. Remember Joe Nicholas? Oh sure, yeah. Yeah, he was, he was with them then. Oh, Lord, that. He meant Louis Cabot. Well, that's not bad, huh? Why you call it that? I went playing, playing along with them. So I went with Chris Kelly and, well, different fellas, you know, I would go around playing with them. Okay, that's good. So, next band I got with was Kid Renee. Well, I stayed with Kid Renee a good while. And I was- That was the brass band or the dance band? No, dance band. Yeah. And I'd leave him and, well, when I left him, I went with, uh, another fella had a band around. Yeah, well, I played with him for pretty good while until got around depression time. When it got around depression, when I just give up playing, stopped all together.
